glossary.definition: A state is the description of how a quantum system is prepared, used to predict the probabilities of measurement outcomes. A pure state can be represented by a ket, a column vector in a chosen basis, or a wave function.
glossary.example: For two chosen basis outcomes, the column (1, 0) predicts the first with certainty; (1, 1)/√2 predicts equal probabilities.

glossary.definition: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Once a basis is chosen, a linear operator can be represented by a matrix acting on a column of vector coordinates.
glossary.example: The matrix with diagonal entries 1 and −1 sends the column (a, b) to (a, −b).

glossary.definition: A column vector is a vertical list of a vector's coordinates in a chosen basis. It represents a ket in the finite-dimensional matrix examples.
glossary.example: The column with entries 1 and i, divided by √2, represents the state used throughout the examples.

glossary.definition: A row vector is a horizontal list of numbers. In an orthonormal basis, a bra is represented by the complex-conjugated transpose of its ket's column vector.
Transposing a matrix exchanges its rows and columns without changing the entries. Taking the adjoint also complex-conjugates those entries.
Matrix multiplication combines a row of the first matrix with a column of the second: multiply corresponding entries and add them. The order of the factors matters.
A vector is an element of a vector space: an object that can be added to other vectors and multiplied by scalars according to the space's rules.
glossary.example: An arrow, an ordered pair and a wave function can each be a vector in an appropriate space.

glossary.definition: A vector space is a set of vectors equipped with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-algebra laws, including closure, associativity and distributivity.
glossary.example: All ordered pairs of real numbers form a vector space; adding two pairs gives another pair.

glossary.definition: A scalar is a number used to multiply a vector. In a complex vector space, scalars are complex numbers.
glossary.example: In 3ψ, the number 3 is a scalar.

glossary.definition: A complex number has the form a + ib, with real a and b and i squared equal to −1. Its complex conjugate is a − ib.
glossary.example: The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 − 3i.

glossary.definition: A linear combination is a sum of vectors multiplied by scalar coefficients.
glossary.example: 2u − 3v is a linear combination of u and v.

glossary.definition: Closure means that performing the specified operation on members of a set always produces a member of that same set.
glossary.example: Adding two plane arrows produces another plane arrow.

glossary.definition: A Hilbert space is a vector space with an inner product that is complete in the resulting norm.
glossary.example: For a particle on a line, the space of square-integrable wave functions is a Hilbert space. Each whole function ψ(x) is one vector.

glossary.definition: An inner product is a scalar-valued pairing of two vectors that defines their overlap, lengths and orthogonality. For complex functions it integrates the conjugate of the first function times the second.
glossary.example: For ordinary real arrows, the dot product is an inner product.

glossary.definition: The norm of a vector is its length. It is the square root of the vector's inner product with itself; that inner product is the squared norm.
glossary.example: The norm of the real pair (3, 4) is 5; its squared norm is 25.

glossary.definition: A Cauchy sequence is a sequence whose terms eventually become arbitrarily close to one another and stay that close.
glossary.example: The numbers 1, 1.1, 1.11, 1.111, … form a Cauchy sequence.

glossary.definition: Completeness means that every Cauchy sequence has a limit that belongs to the space.
glossary.example: A sequence can approximate a wave function more and more closely without its limit falling outside a complete function space.

glossary.definition: A space is separable if it contains a countable dense subset: a countable collection whose members can approximate any vector arbitrarily closely.
A countable set is a finite set or an infinite set whose members can be listed in a sequence indexed by the positive integers.
A dense subset is a selection of vectors from which every vector in the full space can be approximated arbitrarily closely.
A basis is an independent set of vectors whose linear combinations build every vector in the space. An orthonormal basis also has unit norms and zero overlap between different members.
glossary.example: The horizontal and vertical unit arrows form a basis for a plane.

glossary.definition: The dimension of a vector space is the number of vectors in a basis. A function space can have infinitely many basis vectors.
glossary.example: A plane has dimension two.

glossary.definition: Vectors are linearly independent if none can be expressed as a linear combination of the others.
A set spans a space when every vector in that space can be written as a linear combination of the set's members.
Two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is zero. This generalizes perpendicular arrows to complex vectors and functions.
A set is orthonormal when every vector has unit norm and distinct members have zero inner product.
A function is square-integrable when the integral of its squared modulus over its domain is finite. A nonzero such wave function can be normalized.
A wave function is a complex-valued function representing a quantum state in a chosen representation. In position space, its squared modulus gives probability density after normalization.
Normalization is scaling a nonzero state vector to unit norm, so its total probability is one.
A ket is Dirac's notation for a vector representing a quantum state.
glossary.example: The symbol |ψ⟩ names a state vector without choosing position or matrix coordinates.

glossary.definition: A bra is a linear scalar-valued rule acting on kets. The bra associated with a ket is defined by the inner product and has conjugated coefficients.
The dual space is the vector space of linear scalar-valued rules acting on the original space. For a Hilbert space, bras are its continuous linear rules.
glossary.example: If a ket has coordinates (a, b), the rule that returns 2a + 3b is an element of its dual space.

glossary.definition: A bra-ket is the scalar inner product obtained by applying a bra to a ket. It is called an overlap or probability amplitude in state comparisons.
An outer product is an operator formed from a ket followed by a bra. It maps an input ket to the first ket multiplied by the bra's overlap with the input.
An operator is a mathematical rule that takes a vector as input and produces a vector as output.
glossary.example: On wave functions, multiplication by x is an operator.

glossary.definition: A linear operator is an operator that preserves addition and scalar multiplication: processing a linear combination gives the same combination of the processed vectors.
The adjoint of A is the operator defined by conjugating A's inner-product matrix elements and exchanging the two states. In an orthonormal finite basis it is the conjugate transpose.
A Hermitian operator equals its own adjoint on the appropriate domain. It represents an observable in this course and has real expectation values.
An operator is anti-Hermitian when its adjoint is its negative. Its expectation values are purely imaginary or zero.
The domain of an operator is the set of input vectors on which it is defined. For a function it is the set of allowed inputs; boundary conditions can restrict an operator's domain.
An expectation value is the probability-weighted mean of measurement outcomes for identically prepared states.
The identity operator I maps every vector to itself. It plays the role of the number one in operator algebra.
The commutator [A, B] is the operator AB − BA, the difference between applying A and B in the two possible orders.
Two operators commute if their ordered products are equal on the common domain. Their commutator is then zero.
The anticommutator of A and B is the sum of the ordered products, AB + BA.
A superposition is a quantum state formed as a linear combination of state vectors.
An observable is a physical quantity that can be measured, such as position, momentum or energy. This course represents it by a suitable Hermitian operator.
Quantum uncertainty is the standard deviation of measurement outcomes for identically prepared states.
A standard deviation measures spread about the mean: square the deviations, average them with their probabilities, then take the square root.
Variance is the probability-weighted mean of squared deviations from the mean. Its square root is the standard deviation.
An operator function F(A) is an operator built from A using the specified mathematical function. A convergent power series defines it by replacing powers of the variable with powers of A.
A power series is a sum of successive nonnegative integer powers of a variable, each multiplied by a coefficient.
The operator exponential is the operator defined by the exponential power series, I + A + A²/2! + A³/3! + …, wherever that series is defined.
An operator is unitary if its adjoint equals its inverse. It preserves inner products and therefore lengths and probabilities.
An electron gas is a collection of mobile electrons treated as particles occupying states. A filled Fermi sea is the collection of occupied states up to the Fermi energy at zero temperature.
A conduction electron is an electron in a material that can contribute to electric current by changing its occupied state under an applied field.
Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics is the classical distribution of dilute particles over energy states. It does not impose Pauli exclusion.
Fermi–Dirac statistics gives the occupation probability of a single-fermion state at thermal equilibrium, with at most one electron in each complete state.
Pauli exclusion states that no two identical fermions occupy the same complete single-particle quantum state. Two electrons can share a spatial orbital only with different spins.
Drift velocity is the average directed velocity of charge carriers caused by an applied field, superimposed on their random motion.
Momentum relaxation time is the characteristic time over which scattering reduces the average directed carrier momentum.
Mean free path is the average distance a particle travels between relevant scattering events.
Electrical conductivity is the coefficient relating current density to electric field in Ohm's law. Higher conductivity means a larger current density for the same field.
Resistivity measures a material's opposition to current flow. In this scalar model it is the reciprocal of electrical conductivity.
Thermal conductivity is the material coefficient relating heat flow per unit area to a temperature gradient.
Heat capacity is the energy required for a unit increase in temperature under specified conditions. The electronic contribution comes from changes in electron energy.
Classical equipartition assigns an average energy of half k_B T to each independent quadratic energy term in classical equilibrium.
The Sommerfeld model treats a metal's conduction electrons as independent quantum particles in a constant potential, filled according to Pauli exclusion and Fermi–Dirac statistics.
A spatial orbital is a one-electron wave function describing the spatial part of a state. Each orbital permits two electron spin states.
Spin is a particle's intrinsic angular momentum. For an electron, a measurement of one spin component has two possible values, plus or minus hbar/2.
The Fermi energy is the energy of the highest occupied electron state at zero temperature. At finite temperature, the Fermi level commonly refers to the chemical potential.
The chemical potential is the equilibrium energy parameter controlling the change in particle number and the Fermi–Dirac occupation probabilities. It approaches the Fermi energy at zero temperature.
The density of states is the number of available single-electron states per unit energy near a specified energy. Occupation is counted separately.
glossary.example: A mean of 20 states in a 0.1 eV interval corresponds to 200 states per eV.

glossary.definition: The Fermi surface is the boundary in wave-vector space separating occupied from empty states at zero temperature. For an isotropic free gas it is a sphere.
The Fermi temperature is the temperature scale T_F = E_F/k_B associated with the Fermi energy.
A degenerate electron gas is one whose occupations are strongly constrained by Pauli exclusion, typically at temperatures much smaller than its Fermi temperature.
A continuum approximation replaces very closely spaced discrete states with a continuous count or integral when many levels lie in the relevant interval.
A periodic potential is a potential-energy function that repeats after a lattice translation.
An energy band is a continuous interval of allowed electron energies in an ideal macroscopic crystal.
A band gap is an energy interval between bands that contains no allowed bulk one-electron states.
A Bloch wave is a crystal state written as a plane-wave factor multiplied by a lattice-periodic function.
A plane wave has a phase that advances linearly in position and a constant amplitude. In an infinite space it is an idealized, non-square-integrable state.
A wave packet is a localized combination of waves with different wave vectors. Its envelope moves at the group velocity.
A wave vector specifies how wave phase changes with position. In one dimension its magnitude is 2π divided by wavelength.
A reciprocal lattice vector changes a plane wave's phase by an integer multiple of 2π under every direct-lattice translation. It labels equivalent crystal wave vectors.
A Brillouin zone is a region of reciprocal space used to label crystal states. In one dimension, a first zone extends from −π/a to π/a, counting equivalent endpoints only once.
A primitive cell is a smallest repeating cell of a lattice; translating it by lattice vectors reproduces the lattice.
The Kronig–Penney model is a one-dimensional periodic sequence of potential wells and barriers used to demonstrate allowed bands and forbidden gaps.
Effective mass is the mass-like coefficient relating a carrier's acceleration in a crystal band to an external force. In one dimension its inverse is band curvature divided by hbar squared.
Group velocity is the velocity of a wave packet's envelope. For a crystal electron it equals the band-energy slope divided by hbar.
Crystal momentum is hbar times the Bloch wave vector. It labels a crystal state and changes under an applied force; it need not equal ordinary mechanical momentum.
Band curvature is the second derivative of energy with respect to wave vector. It describes how rapidly the band slope changes and sets the inverse effective mass.
An inflection point is a point where a curve changes its direction of curvature. For a smooth ordinary band, its second derivative vanishes there.
A metal is a material with readily mobile charge carriers; in the ordinary band picture it has partially filled or overlapping bands with accessible states at the Fermi energy.
A semiconductor is a material whose carrier population and conductivity can be strongly controlled by temperature, light or doping. Its band gap separates valence and conduction bands.
An insulator is a material with very few mobile carriers under ordinary conditions. In the ordinary band picture its filled and empty bands are separated by a poorly accessible gap.
The conduction band is the band above the valence-band gap that can hold mobile electrons in an ordinary semiconductor or insulator.
The valence band is the highest filled electron band in the ideal zero-temperature semiconductor or insulator.
An intrinsic semiconductor is undoped material whose equilibrium mobile electrons and holes are generated in equal numbers by pair excitation.
An extrinsic semiconductor is material intentionally doped with impurity atoms that alter its mobile-carrier population.
Doping is the deliberate addition of a small controlled quantity of impurity atoms to change a semiconductor's carrier population.
A donor is a dopant that can release an electron into the conduction band. A shallow donor level lies just below the conduction-band edge.
An acceptor is a dopant that can take a valence electron and leave a mobile hole. A shallow acceptor level lies just above the valence-band edge.
A hole is an unoccupied electron state in an otherwise nearly full band, treated as a positive mobile charge carrier.
An n-type semiconductor is donor-doped material in which electrons are the majority mobile carriers.
A p-type semiconductor is acceptor-doped material in which holes are the majority mobile carriers.
Majority carriers are the more numerous mobile carrier type: electrons in n-type material or holes in p-type material.
Minority carriers are the less numerous mobile carrier type: holes in n-type material or electrons in p-type material.
Carrier generation is the creation of mobile electrons and holes by excitation, such as transferring a valence electron into the conduction band.
Recombination is the removal of an electron–hole pair when a conduction electron fills an available valence-band state, releasing energy.
The zero vector is the vector that leaves every vector unchanged when added to it. In a function space, it is the function that is zero everywhere.

Probability density is a function whose integral over a region gives the probability of finding a continuous measurement outcome in that region. A normalized position wave function has density equal to its squared modulus.
A probability amplitude is a complex number whose squared modulus gives the probability of the specified outcome. An overlap with a normalized reference state is one example.
A matrix element is one entry describing an operator relative to chosen basis vectors. It is the overlap of one basis vector with the operator acting on another.
A boundary condition specifies how a function behaves at the edges of its domain or at an interface. It helps select the physically allowed solutions of an equation.
An infinite box is an ideal potential well with infinitely high walls. The particle is confined inside, and its wave function vanishes at the walls.
Cauchy–Schwarz is the inequality stating that the squared modulus of the inner product of two vectors cannot exceed the product of their squared norms.
Robertson's relation bounds the product of two observables' standard deviations below by half the modulus of the expectation of their commutator.
The Jacobi identity is the rule that the cyclic sum [A,[B,C]] + [B,[C,A]] + [C,[A,B]] is zero.
The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula expresses a product of operator exponentials as one exponential involving the operators and their nested commutators.
Bloch's theorem states that energy states in a periodic crystal potential can be chosen as a plane-wave factor times a lattice-periodic function.
The Wiedemann–Franz law relates a metal's electronic thermal conductivity to its electrical conductivity: their ratio is approximately proportional to absolute temperature.
Phase specifies a wave's position within its oscillation. Multiplication by a unit-modulus complex phase changes the wave's complex angle without changing its squared amplitude.

sections.title: Quantum Mechanics I · Spaces, notation and operators

sheets.title: Hilbert space, basis and wave functions
sheets.source: Zettili, 2nd ed., §§2.2.1–2.2.4, pp.79–84; FYUGP Semester V, Module III, Unit 12.

cards.title: State · the description used for predictions
cards.meaning: A state is the description of how a quantum system is prepared, used to predict the probabilities of measurement outcomes.
cards.picture: For a system with two chosen basis outcomes, represent a pure state by a two-entry column vector. The entries are probability amplitudes; their squared magnitudes give the two probabilities.
cards.example: The column (1, 0) gives the first basis outcome with certainty. The column (1, i)/√2 gives each basis outcome with probability 1/2.
cards.bridge: A ket names the state without choosing coordinates. A column vector or wave function describes that state in a chosen representation.

cards.title: Vector space · in plain words
cards.meaning: A vector space is a collection of vectors together with rules for adding and scaling them.
cards.picture: Start with all two-entry complex column vectors. Add columns entry by entry and multiply each entry by the same scalar to scale a vector. These operations stay in the same collection.
cards.example: The columns (1, 0) and (0, 1) can build any column (a, b). A whole wave function ψ(x) can also be one vector in a function space.
cards.bridge: The matrix examples give a finite-dimensional picture; the formal vector-space rules also apply to wave functions.

cards.label: QM · 1 of 6 · 30 min
cards.title: What is a vector space?
cards.body: A vector space is a set of objects called vectors, with rules for adding them and multiplying them by numbers (scalars), obeying the vector-algebra laws. In a complex vector space, the scalars may be complex.

cards.title: Hilbert space · a space of wave functions
cards.meaning: For a particle on a line, picture a Hilbert space as the collection of all square-integrable wave functions ψ(x). Each whole function is one vector in this space.
cards.picture: A point in an ordinary plane is described by two coordinates. A vector in this function space is described by its values across x. Adding two functions or scaling one produces another function in the space.
cards.example: A decaying wave packet belongs to this space when the integral of its squared amplitude is finite.
cards.bridge: We also need an inner product to compare functions and completeness so that convergent approximations have their limits inside the space. Nonzero functions can be normalized to represent states.

cards.title: What is a Hilbert space?
cards.body: A Hilbert space is a vector space with an inner product and all its Cauchy limits. A Cauchy sequence has terms that eventually stay arbitrarily close to each other; completeness keeps its limit in the space.

cards.title: Inner product and norm
cards.body: An inner product is a scalar assigned to a pair of vectors; the norm \(\|\psi\|=\sqrt{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle}\) is the vector's length. This product is linear in the ket and conjugate-linear in the bra, with \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle=\langle\psi|\phi\rangle^*\). The state spaces here are also separable: every vector can be approximated arbitrarily closely by members of a countable set.

cards.title: What are basis and dimension?
cards.body: A basis is a set of independent vectors from which every vector in the space can be built by a linear combination. The dimension is the number of vectors in a basis.

cards.title: Matrix picture · two coordinates
cards.body: The two columns \(e_1,e_2\) form an orthonormal basis. The state is \(\psi=(e_1+i e_2)/\sqrt2\). Its inner product with itself is \((1+(-i)i)/2=1\), so it is normalized. We will reuse this same state in the next matrix examples.

cards.title: Orthonormal basis and spanning
cards.body: Independent means no member can be built from the others; spanning means their combinations reach every vector. Orthonormal means mutually perpendicular with unit norm. In an orthonormal basis spanning the space, \(c_n=\langle e_n|\psi\rangle\) and \(\|\psi\|^2=\sum_n|c_n|^2\). Two independent vectors cannot span a three-dimensional space.

cards.title: What is a square-integrable function?
cards.body: A square-integrable function has a finite integral of its squared modulus over its domain. A nonzero such wave function can be normalized. A constant-amplitude plane wave on the whole real line fails this condition.

cards.title: Normalize an exponential wave function
cards.legend: \(\psi(x)=A e^{-\alpha|x|}\), \(\alpha>0\); choose \(A\) real and positive. The overall phase is arbitrary.

steps.note: A normalized state has total probability one.
Square the modulus, not the amplitude itself.

ask.q: Which quantity is the probability density?
ask.why: Probability density is the squared modulus, a real nonnegative quantity.

steps.note: The integrand is even.

ask.q: Why double the positive-half integral?
ask.why: An even integrand has equal contributions from the two halves.

steps.note: The exponential vanishes at infinity.

ask.q: Which condition makes the integral finite?
ask.why: Positive alpha gives decaying tails.

steps.note: Isolate the squared amplitude.
Choose the positive amplitude as a phase convention.

ask.q: Which positive real A normalizes this wave function?
ask.why: Normalization fixes the modulus; a phase convention selects the positive root.

cards.title: Normalize a finite vector
cards.body: For orthonormal \(e_1,e_2\), divide by 5. The normalized coefficients are \(3/5\) and \(4i/5\), whose squared moduli sum to one.

cards.q: Which property distinguishes a Hilbert space from a general inner-product space?
cards.why: Completeness ensures that Cauchy sequences converge to elements inside the space.

cards.q: A linearly independent spanning set is a ____.
cards.why: Independence prevents redundancy; spanning ensures all vectors can be expanded.

cards.q: For orthonormal basis vectors, what is the squared norm of \(2|e_1\rangle-i|e_2\rangle\)?
cards.why: Cross terms vanish, leaving \(|2|^2+|-i|^2=5\).

sheets.title: Kets, bras and bra-kets
sheets.source: Zettili §2.3, pp.84–89; FYUGP Module III, Unit 13.

cards.title: Kets and bras · in plain words
cards.meaning: A ket is a way of writing a quantum state vector. A bra is a matching rule that compares another state with that vector and returns a number.
cards.picture: In an orthonormal matrix basis, write a ket as a column. Its bra is the corresponding row with complex-conjugated entries. Multiplying that row by a ket column gives an overlap.
cards.example: For the ket column (1, i)/√2, the matching bra row is (1, −i)/√2. Their product is one.
cards.bridge: The dual space is the collection of linear comparison rules represented here by rows. A state is the preparation description used to predict outcomes.

cards.label: QM · 2 of 6 · 20 min
cards.title: What are a ket and a bra?
cards.body: A ket is a symbol for a state vector. Its bra is the associated linear rule that takes a ket as input and returns a scalar inner product; conjugate all coefficients when converting a ket to its bra.

cards.title: Matrix picture · column, row, number
cards.body: Conjugate and transpose the column to get the bra row. Row-by-column multiplication gives \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=(1+(-i)i)/2=1\). The result is one number, so a bra-ket is a scalar.

cards.title: Conjugate the coefficients
cards.body: The dual space is the space of linear scalar-valued rules acting on kets; a bra is one such rule. Reversing the bracket alone is insufficient: real coefficients stay fixed, but complex coefficients must be conjugated.

cards.title: What is a bra-ket?
cards.body: A bra-ket is the inner product of two state vectors: a scalar called their overlap. Zero overlap means orthogonality. For normalized states, its squared modulus is the probability of the associated state test.

cards.title: Inner-product rules
cards.body: Order matters: \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle=\langle\psi|\phi\rangle^*\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2\leq\|\phi\|^2\|\psi\|^2\).

cards.title: Evaluate an overlap
cards.body: Take \(|\psi\rangle=(|e_1\rangle+i|e_2\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \(|\phi\rangle=(|e_1\rangle-|e_2\rangle)/\sqrt2\). Orthonormality removes the cross terms. The probability is \(1/2\).

cards.title: What is an outer product?
cards.body: An outer product is an operator made by placing a ket before a bra. It sends an input ket to the first ket multiplied by the scalar overlap with the bra.

cards.title: Matrix picture · reverse the multiplication
cards.body: Column-by-row multiplication produces a matrix rather than a single number. Each entry is a column entry times a row entry. Acting this matrix on a column produces another column, which is how an operator acts on a ket.

cards.title: Orthogonal versus orthonormal
cards.body: Orthogonal means zero overlap for distinct states. Orthonormal adds unit norm for each. The triangle inequality is \(\|\phi+\psi\|\leq\|\phi\|+\|\psi\|\).

cards.q: What kind of mathematical object is \(|\phi\rangle\langle\psi|\)?
cards.why: It maps an input ket to another ket multiplied by an overlap.

cards.q: Two nonzero states with zero inner product are ____.
cards.why: Zero overlap defines orthogonality; unit norm is a separate condition.

cards.q: For normalized states, \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle=3i/5\). What is the probability of the phi state test?
cards.why: The probability is the modulus squared, \(9/25=0.36\).

sheets.title: Operators and the Hermitian adjoint
sheets.source: Zettili §§2.4.1–2.4.2, pp.89–92; FYUGP Module III, Unit 14.

cards.title: Operator · a rule acting on a state
cards.meaning: An operator is a mathematical rule that takes a vector as input and produces a vector as output.
cards.picture: For a wave function, multiplying by x is one rule; differentiating with respect to x is another. A linear rule treats a sum the same way whether you process the sum at once or its parts separately.
cards.example: The position operator sends ψ(x) to xψ(x).
cards.bridge: Operators are mathematical objects. Applying an operator is not automatically the same as performing a physical measurement.

cards.label: QM · 3 of 6 · 25 min
cards.title: What is a linear operator?
cards.body: An operator is a rule that maps vectors to vectors. It is linear when applying it to a sum of scaled vectors gives the same result as applying it to each vector and then adding the scaled results.

cards.title: Matrix picture · an operator acts on a column
cards.body: For this example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). Row-by-column multiplication leaves the first coordinate unchanged and reverses the sign of the second. The input and output are both vectors in the same two-dimensional space.

cards.title: Position and momentum operators
cards.body: The position operator multiplies a wave function by x; momentum differentiates it and multiplies by minus i hbar. In AB, B acts first. Products are associative but generally do not commute. The identity leaves a state unchanged. The expectation (mean outcome) is \(\langle A\rangle=\langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle/\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\).

cards.title: Adjoint · the matching operator
cards.meaning: The adjoint is the operator matched to A by the inner product: it gives the corresponding conjugated overlap when the two comparison states are exchanged.
cards.picture: For a matrix in an orthonormal basis, swap rows with columns and conjugate every entry. The resulting matrix is the adjoint.
cards.example: A real symmetric matrix is unchanged by this procedure, so it is Hermitian.
cards.bridge: An adjoint is defined by inner products; it does not generally undo A as an inverse would.

cards.title: What is the Hermitian adjoint?
cards.body: The adjoint of A is the operator A† whose matrix elements are the complex conjugates of A's matrix elements with the two states exchanged. In an orthonormal finite basis, take the conjugate transpose.

cards.title: Matrix picture · transpose, then conjugate
cards.body: Transpose moves the off-diagonal i to the lower-left entry; conjugation changes it to −i. These matrices differ, so M is not Hermitian. In contrast, the real diagonal matrix \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) equals its own adjoint.

cards.title: Adjoint rules
cards.body: Also \((A+B)^\dagger=A^\dagger+B^\dagger\) and \((A^\dagger)^\dagger=A\). Reverse the whole product order, conjugate scalars and adjoint every factor.

cards.title: What is a Hermitian operator?
cards.body: A Hermitian operator is a linear operator equal to its own adjoint. Its expectation values are real. For a differential operator, the domain includes the boundary conditions needed for that equality.

cards.title: When is a product Hermitian?
cards.body: Thus AB is Hermitian when A and B commute (with compatible domains). Their sum is Hermitian without a commutation condition.

cards.title: Why a Hermitian expectation is real

phases.name: Conjugate
phases.why: compare an expectation with its conjugate

phases.name: Reality
phases.why: equality with a conjugate implies reality

steps.note: Name the expectation z.
Consider the complex conjugate.

ask.q: What should be compared with z to test reality?
ask.why: A scalar is real precisely when it equals its conjugate.

steps.note: Apply the adjoint definition.

ask.q: Which operator appears in the conjugated sandwich?
ask.why: The adjoint is defined by conjugating matrix elements.

steps.note: Use Hermiticity.

ask.q: Which property of A is needed at this step?
options: It is diagonal in every basis
ask.why: Hermiticity allows replacement of the adjoint by A.

steps.note: Its imaginary part must vanish.

ask.q: What follows from this equality?
ask.why: A complex number equals its conjugate only if its imaginary part is zero.

cards.title: Complex scalars change Hermiticity
cards.body: A real multiple remains Hermitian; a purely imaginary multiple is anti-Hermitian. For example, \((2iAB)^\dagger=-2iB^\dagger A^\dagger\).

cards.q: Which is the adjoint of \(AB\)?
cards.why: Taking an adjoint reverses the order of the factors.

cards.q: An operator equal to its adjoint is called ____.
cards.why: In finite dimensions Hermitian and self-adjoint coincide; infinite-dimensional domains require care.

cards.q: Two Hermitian operators A and B have a Hermitian product AB when which condition holds?
cards.why: Since \((AB)^\dagger=BA\), equality with AB requires \(AB=BA\).

sections.title: Quantum Mechanics I · Commutators, uncertainty and operator functions

sheets.title: Commutator algebra
sheets.source: Zettili §2.4.4, pp.93–95; FYUGP Module III, Unit 15.

cards.title: Commutator · compare two orders
cards.meaning: A commutator is the difference between doing two operations in one order and doing them in the reverse order.
cards.picture: Apply B and then A; separately apply A and then B. Subtract the two results. If the difference is always zero, the operations commute.
cards.example: Differentiating x times a function gives an extra term compared with multiplying x by the derivative.
cards.bridge: The operator AB means B acts first. The commutator is AB − BA.

cards.label: QM · 4 of 6 · 24 min
cards.title: What is a commutator?
cards.body: The commutator of A and B is the operator AB − BA: the difference between the two ordered products. A zero commutator means that swapping their order does not change their action on allowed states.

cards.title: Matrix picture · order changes the result
cards.body: B swaps the two coordinates; A reverses the second coordinate's sign. On \(e_1=(1,0)^T\), \(ABe_1=(0,-1)^T\) while \(BAe_1=(0,1)^T\). Their difference is nonzero, so the operations do not commute.

cards.title: Basic identities
cards.body: Also \([A,A]=0\), \([A,cI]=0\), and \([aA,bB]=ab[A,B]\) for scalars. The anticommutator is \(\{A,B\}=AB+BA\).

cards.title: Derive the product rule
cards.legend: A, B and C are operators with a common domain for the products shown.

steps.note: Apply the definition with BC as one operator.
Insert minus BAC plus BAC.

ask.q: Which insertion helps without changing the expression?
ask.why: The inserted pair is zero and allows adjacent pairs to be factored.

steps.note: Factor C on the right of the first pair.

ask.q: Where must the common C remain?
ask.why: Moving C across other operators would assume commutation.

steps.note: Factor B on the left of the second pair.

ask.q: What is the second common factor?
ask.why: BAC and BCA share B in the leftmost position.

steps.note: Replace the first difference by a commutator.
The order of both products is retained.

ask.q: Which is the correct final product rule?
ask.why: Each commutator replaces exactly the corresponding ordered difference.

cards.title: Other useful algebra rules
cards.body: The Jacobi identity is \([A,[B,C]]+[B,[C,A]]+[C,[A,B]]=0\). Also \([A,B]^\dagger=[B^\dagger,A^\dagger]\); for Hermitian A and B the commutator is anti-Hermitian.

cards.title: Derive the position–momentum commutator
cards.legend: \(p=-i\hbar\,d/dx\). Apply both sides to an arbitrary differentiable test function \(f(x)\).

phases.name: Act
phases.why: test an operator identity on a function

phases.name: Differentiate
phases.why: the product rule differentiates x too

steps.note: Apply the commutator definition.
The second minus sign changes sign.

ask.q: In p(xf), what does the derivative act on?
ask.why: The momentum operator differentiates everything to its right in the product.

steps.note: Use the derivative product rule.

ask.q: What is the derivative of xf?
ask.why: Both x and f depend on x; the derivative of x is one.

steps.note: Distribute the factor i hbar.
The two terms containing f prime cancel.

ask.q: Which terms cancel?
options: The two terms in xf prime
ask.why: Their magnitudes match and their signs are opposite.

steps.note: The identity holds on every allowed test function.

ask.q: Which operator multiplies every test function by itself?
ask.why: The surviving action is multiplication by i hbar times the identity.

cards.title: Use the product rule twice
cards.body: Since \(i\hbar I\) commutes with p, the two terms combine. In contrast, \([x,p_y]=0\): differentiation with respect to y does not act on x.

cards.title: Powers keep their order
cards.body: Only if \([A,B]\) commutes with B can this simplify to \(n[A,B]B^{n-1}\). Do not apply a scalar power rule to general operators.

cards.q: If A and B are Hermitian, what is the commutator \([A,B]\)?
cards.why: Its adjoint is \([B,A]=-[A,B]\).

cards.q: Operators with zero commutator are said to ____.
cards.why: A zero commutator means that the two products AB and BA agree.

cards.q: In \([x,p^3]=c\,i\hbar p^2\), what is c?
cards.why: The product rule supplies three identical terms because \([x,p]=i\hbar I\).

sheets.title: Uncertainty between two operators
sheets.source: Zettili §2.4.5, pp.95–96; FYUGP Module III, Unit 16.

cards.title: Uncertainty · the spread of outcomes
cards.meaning: Uncertainty is a number describing how widely measurement outcomes are spread around their mean for the same prepared state.
cards.picture: Prepare the same state many times and measure once on each preparation. A narrow distribution has small uncertainty; a broad distribution has large uncertainty.
cards.example: A position distribution with a standard deviation of 1 nm has position uncertainty 1 nm.
cards.bridge: For suitable pairs of observables, quantum mechanics puts a lower bound on the product of their standard deviations.

cards.label: QM · 5 of 6 · 25 min
cards.title: What is uncertainty?
cards.body: The uncertainty of an observable is its standard deviation: the root-mean-square spread of repeated outcomes about their mean in identically prepared states. This is a property of the prepared state.

cards.title: Center the operators
cards.tex: \delta A=A-\langle A\rangle I\qquad\delta B=B-\langle B\rangle I
cards.body: The centered operators are Hermitian, have zero expectation and satisfy \([\delta A,\delta B]=[A,B]\). Their squared expectations are the variances.

cards.title: Start from Cauchy–Schwarz
cards.body: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to \(|u\rangle=\delta A|\psi\rangle\) and \(|v\rangle=\delta B|\psi\rangle\). Their norms squared are the two variances.

cards.title: Separate the commutator contribution
cards.legend: Let \(z=\langle\delta A\delta B\rangle\). Define real \(C=\langle\{\delta A,\delta B\}\rangle\) and real \(K=-i\langle[A,B]\rangle\).

phases.name: Expect
phases.why: Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts give real and imaginary terms

phases.name: Modulus
phases.why: sum the squares of real and imaginary parts

steps.note: This is the overlap appearing in Cauchy–Schwarz.

move.by: \delta A\delta B=\tfrac12\{\delta A,\delta B\}+\tfrac12[\delta A,\delta B]

steps.note: The sum of the two operator parts is the original product.

ask.q: Which split recovers an ordered product AB?
options: Half its anticommutator plus half its commutator
The product of the two brackets
ask.why: Adding AB+BA and AB−BA leaves 2AB.

steps.note: Scalar expectation values commute with everything.

ask.q: Why does centering leave the commutator unchanged?
ask.why: Subtracting a scalar multiple of I adds no commutator terms.

steps.note: The anticommutator is Hermitian, so C is real.

ask.q: Why is C real?
ask.why: For Hermitian centered operators, the adjoint of their anticommutator is itself.

steps.note: An anti-Hermitian expectation is purely imaginary.
Multiply z by its conjugate.

ask.q: How is the modulus squared evaluated?
ask.why: The modulus squared is z star times z, so it is real and nonnegative.

steps.note: Mixed terms cancel and i squared is minus one.

cards.title: The general uncertainty relation
cards.body: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the variance product by \(|z|^2\). Dropping the nonnegative \(C^2/4\) gives the squared bound; taking nonnegative square roots yields Robertson's relation.

cards.title: Matrix picture · calculate the spreads
cards.body: Use the previous matrices \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) and B that swaps coordinates, with \(\psi=(1,i)^T/\sqrt2\). Matrix multiplication gives \(\langle A\rangle=\langle B\rangle=0\) and \(A^2=B^2=I\), so both variances are one. The Robertson bound is \(|2i|/2=1\), equal to \(\Delta A\Delta B\). These dimensionless matrices illustrate the general relation, not the canonical position–momentum pair.

cards.title: Heisenberg position–momentum relations
cards.body: Insert \([x,p_x]=i\hbar I\) and \(\langle I\rangle=1\). The same lower bound holds for y and z pairs. The Robertson lower bound for \(x,p_y\) is zero.

cards.title: A zero bound is not a zero spread
cards.body: If the commutator expectation vanishes, Robertson's lower bound is zero. This alone does not say that either variance vanishes. Equality requires special states, not every wave function.

cards.title: Estimate a momentum spread
cards.body: For \(\Delta x=0.10\) nm, this is the minimum possible spread. It is a lower bound, so an actual state may have a larger spread.

cards.q: What does \(\Delta A\) represent in the uncertainty relation?
cards.why: It is the statistical spread in repeated measurements on the same prepared state.

cards.q: The general bound involves the expectation of the ____ of A and B.
cards.why: The antisymmetric operator part gives the Robertson lower bound.

cards.q: Using units with \(\hbar=1\), if \(\Delta x=0.25\), what is the minimum allowed \(\Delta p_x\)?
cards.why: Divide \(1/2\) by 0.25 to obtain 2.

sheets.title: Functions of operators
sheets.source: Zettili §2.4.6, p.97; FYUGP Module III, Unit 17.

cards.title: Operator function · build a new rule
cards.meaning: A function of an operator is an operator constructed from an existing operator according to a specified mathematical function.
cards.picture: If A is a rule, A squared means apply that rule twice. A polynomial combines repeated applications with addition and scaling; a convergent power series extends this idea.
cards.example: For F(t) = 1 + t + t², the operator version is F(A) = I + A + A².
cards.bridge: The constant term becomes a multiple of the identity, so the whole expression still acts on vectors.

cards.label: QM · 6 of 6 · 20 min
cards.title: What is a function of an operator?
cards.body: An operator function F(A) is a rule for constructing a new operator from A. For a convergent power series, replace its variable by A, its constant term by a multiple of I, and use the same coefficients.

cards.title: Matrix picture · a polynomial of A
cards.body: For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), direct multiplication gives \(A^2=I\). Thus \(F(A)=2I+A\). On the same state, \(F(A)\psi=(3,i)^T/\sqrt2\). The output is not normalized; a general operator need not preserve norm.

cards.title: The operator exponential
cards.body: The operator exponential is the operator defined by this series wherever it converges on the states considered. Its first term is the identity I. Functions of the same operator commute: \([F(A),G(A)]=0\).

cards.title: Commuting with a function
cards.body: If \([B,A]=0\), every power commutes with B and hence so does F(A). The converse need not hold: a constant function commutes with every operator.

cards.title: Adjoint of an operator function
cards.body: For Hermitian A, real-coefficient power series give Hermitian operators. A complex function of a Hermitian operator need not be Hermitian: \((iA)^\dagger=-iA\).

cards.title: Expand an exponential with A squared equal to I
cards.legend: \(A^2=I\), real \(\theta\). This is a power-series example, not a new eigenvalue topic.

phases.name: Powers
phases.why: even powers become I and odd powers become A

steps.note: Start from the exponential series.
Separate even and odd terms.

ask.q: Which split exploits A squared equal to I?
ask.why: Even powers reduce to I, while odd powers reduce to A.

steps.note: Replace each even power by I.

ask.q: What is A to the power 2r?
ask.why: Every pair of A factors equals I.

steps.note: Replace each odd power by A.

ask.q: What is A to the power 2r+1?
ask.why: After removing r pairs, one A remains.

steps.note: The even terms are the cosine series.
The odd terms are i times the sine series.

ask.q: Which function comes from the odd series?
ask.why: Odd powers of i alternate as i, minus i, i, producing i times sine.

cards.title: Do not combine noncommuting exponentials
cards.body: Generally this equality fails. If \([A,B]\) commutes with both A and B, the special BCH form is \(e^Ae^B=e^{A+B+[A,B]/2}\); without that condition, more nested terms are needed.

cards.title: Conjugation by an exponential
cards.body: This nested-commutator identity follows by expanding the exponentials. If \([A,B]=0\), it leaves B unchanged. If the second nested commutator vanishes, the series stops after the first.

cards.title: A short exponential example
cards.body: Substitute \(\cos(\pi/2)=0\) and \(\sin(\pi/2)=1\) into the derived identity.

cards.q: What replaces the constant term 1 in a power series of an operator?
cards.why: The zeroth power is I, which leaves each vector unchanged.

cards.q: The series for the operator exponential contains factorials in the ____.
cards.why: Each nth-order term is divided by n factorial, as in the scalar exponential series.

cards.q: If B commutes with A, which statement follows for a convergent power series F(A)?
cards.why: B commutes with each power of A and therefore with their convergent sum.

sections.title: Properties of Solids · Classical and quantum free electrons

sheets.title: Drude–Lorentz classical theory
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar, Solid State Physics and Electronics, 3rd ed., §5.1, pp.151–153; FYUGP Module II, Unit 6.

cards.title: Electron gas · mobile electrons in a solid
cards.meaning: An electron gas is the collection of conduction electrons that can move through a material.
cards.picture: In the Drude model, treat these electrons as independent classical particles among fixed positive ion cores. A field gives their random motion a small average drift.
cards.example: The mobile conduction electrons in a metal are modeled as an electron gas even though the metal itself is solid.
cards.bridge: Drude–Lorentz uses classical statistics and a constant interior potential. Sommerfeld later replaces the classical occupations with quantum ones.

cards.label: Solids · 1 of 9 · 16 min
cards.title: What is a classical electron gas?
cards.body: An electron gas is a collection of mobile conduction electrons in a solid. Drude–Lorentz treats them as independent classical particles in a constant interior potential, using Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics.

cards.title: What is drift velocity?
cards.body: Drift velocity is the average directed velocity of charge carriers in an applied field. Random thermal motion averages to zero; collisions reduce the directed motion over a momentum-relaxation time tau.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Ion cores and an electron drifting opposite the electric field"><circle cx="50" cy="55" r="15" class="s ok"/><circle cx="130" cy="55" r="15" class="s ok"/><circle cx="210" cy="55" r="15" class="s ok"/><circle cx="50" cy="125" r="15" class="s ok"/><circle cx="130" cy="125" r="15" class="s ok"/><circle cx="210" cy="125" r="15" class="s ok"/><polyline points="160,86 135,97 112,82 88,93" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="88" cy="93" r="5" class="f"/><line x1="85" y1="25" x2="185" y2="25" class="hk" stroke-width="3"/><text x="200" y="30" class="t" font-size="13">E →</text><text x="130" y="165" class="t" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">Electron drift ←</text></svg>

cards.title: Relaxation-time equation
cards.body: Here \(e>0\) is the magnitude of electron charge, m the electron mass and \(\tau\) the momentum relaxation time. The damping term models the mean effect of collisions.

cards.title: Obtain Ohm's law from the model
cards.legend: Steady uniform DC field, electron number density n, electron charge \(-e\). All velocities are mean drift velocities.

phases.name: Current
phases.why: multiply charge by density and velocity

steps.note: Set the mean acceleration to zero.

ask.q: Which quantity vanishes in a steady mean drift?
ask.why: The mean drift is constant when electric acceleration balances relaxation.

steps.note: Move the electric force term to the other side.
Electron drift opposes the field.

ask.q: Why does the drift have a minus sign?
ask.why: The electron force is minus e times the field.

steps.note: Current density is charge density times drift velocity.

ask.q: What converts electron drift to conventional current density?
ask.why: The electron charge density is minus ne.

steps.note: The two negative signs cancel.
Identify the coefficient of the electric field.

ask.q: What happens to conductivity if tau doubles at fixed n?
ask.why: The model conductivity is directly proportional to relaxation time.

cards.title: Resistance and mean free path
cards.body: A longer relaxation time means lower resistivity. The speed used for an estimated mean free path must match the model; classical thermal speed differs from the quantum Fermi speed.

cards.title: What the classical model explains
cards.body: It accounts qualitatively for Ohm's law and high electrical and thermal conductivity. The Wiedemann–Franz relation links thermal to electrical conductivity at a fixed temperature.

cards.title: Where the classical model fails
cards.body: Classical equipartition overestimates electronic heat capacity. The model also fails on magnetic response and detailed temperature dependence, and cannot explain insulating versus metallic band filling.

cards.title: Conductivity example
cards.body: The relaxation-time approximation gives \(\rho\approx3.56\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\mathrm m\). Check the units and use e as a positive magnitude.

cards.q: Which statistics does the Drude–Lorentz classical model use?
cards.why: The classical treatment precedes the use of Pauli exclusion and Fermi–Dirac occupations.

cards.q: The mean time characterizing decay of drift momentum is the ____ time.
cards.why: Tau summarizes momentum loss through scattering in the model.

cards.q: If n and tau each double while m stays fixed, by what factor does Drude conductivity change?
cards.why: Conductivity is proportional to the product n times tau.

sheets.title: Sommerfeld gas in one dimension
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §5.2.1, pp.153–159; FYUGP Module II, Unit 7.

cards.title: Sommerfeld model · fill quantum states
cards.meaning: The Sommerfeld model is a quantum model of the mobile electrons in a metal.
cards.picture: Imagine a ladder of allowed electron states. Electrons fill from the bottom, but each complete state can hold only one electron. This changes the distribution from a classical gas.
cards.example: A spatial box orbital can hold two electrons because it has two different spin states.
cards.bridge: Electrons are still treated as independent and the interior potential is constant; Pauli exclusion and Fermi–Dirac statistics determine filling.

cards.label: Solids · 2 of 9 · 20 min
cards.title: What is the Sommerfeld model?
cards.body: The Sommerfeld model is a quantum gas model of a metal's conduction electrons. They move independently in a constant interior potential but occupy states according to Pauli exclusion and Fermi–Dirac statistics.

cards.title: The one-dimensional box
cards.body: Approximate a line of length L by zero potential inside and infinite barriers at both ends. The wave function vanishes at x = 0 and x = L.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Infinite one-dimensional box and its ground state wave function"><polyline points="45,25 45,140 220,140 220,25" class="lk" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M45 140 Q132.5 -20 220 140" class="hk" stroke-width="3"/><text x="45" y="163" class="t" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">0</text><text x="220" y="163" class="t" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">L</text><text x="132" y="27" class="t" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">ψ₁ schematic</text><text x="132" y="130" class="t" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">V = 0</text></svg>

cards.title: Quantize the box energy
cards.legend: Inside \(0<x<L\), \(V=0\), \(k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar\), and the state is nonzero.

phases.name: Energy
phases.why: allowed wave numbers determine the energies

steps.note: Start from the time-independent Schrödinger equation.
Introduce the positive wave number.

ask.q: Which kind of solution occurs for positive E in the well?
ask.why: The second derivative is minus a positive constant times the function.

steps.note: Write the general solution of the differential equation.
The sine vanishes and the cosine is one at x = 0.

ask.q: Which coefficient vanishes at the first wall?
ask.why: At x = 0 only the cosine term survives.

steps.note: Impose the second wall.
A nonzero state requires a sine node, with positive integer n.

ask.q: Why is n = 0 excluded?
options: It gives the zero wave function
ask.why: With B = 0 and k = 0, the entire sine solution vanishes.

steps.note: Convert the allowed wave number to energy.
The energies rise as n squared.

ask.q: What happens to each energy when L doubles?
ask.why: Every energy scales as the inverse square of box length.

cards.title: Normalize the standing waves
cards.body: Because \(\int_0^L\sin^2(n\pi x/L)dx=L/2\), the prefactor gives unit norm. Distinct n values have orthogonal wave functions.

cards.title: What is a spatial orbital?
cards.body: A spatial orbital is a wave function describing an electron's spatial state. It has two spin states; Pauli exclusion permits one electron per complete spin–orbital state, so each orbital holds at most two.

cards.title: Fill levels from the bottom
cards.body: At zero temperature, two electrons fill each of n = 1, 2, 3, 4. For odd N, the last occupied spatial level has one electron; \(n_F=\lceil N/2\rceil\).

cards.title: Why macroscopic levels look continuous
cards.body: The spacing is finite but very small for a macroscopic box. Increasing L reduces the spacings. A continuum approximation is appropriate when many levels lie in the energy interval of interest.

cards.q: How many electrons can occupy one spatial box orbital?
cards.why: There are two spin states, each occupied at most once.

cards.q: Sommerfeld uses ____–Dirac statistics.
cards.why: Fermi–Dirac statistics enforce Pauli exclusion for electrons.

cards.q: What is \(E_3/E_1\) in the one-dimensional infinite box?
cards.why: The energy is proportional to n squared.

sheets.title: Fermi energy, DOS and filling
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §§5.2.1–5.2.2, pp.156–168; FYUGP Module II, Unit 8, including total energy.

cards.title: Fermi energy · the top occupied level
cards.meaning: The Fermi energy is the energy of the highest occupied electron state at zero temperature.
cards.picture: Fill the allowed states from the bottom upward. The energy at the top of that filled collection is the Fermi energy.
cards.example: Eight electrons in a one-dimensional box fill four spatial levels; the fourth level sets the Fermi energy.
cards.bridge: The total energy adds the energies of all occupied states, so its average per electron is different from the Fermi energy.

cards.label: Solids · 3 of 9 · 24 min
cards.title: What is the Fermi energy?
cards.body: The Fermi energy is the energy of the highest occupied electron state at zero temperature. It is found by filling the available states from lowest to highest energy, subject to Pauli exclusion.

cards.title: Density of states · count the places available
cards.meaning: The density of states tells you how many electron states are available per unit energy near a chosen energy.
cards.picture: Imagine sorting allowed states into narrow energy bins. A bin with more states has a higher density of states. Whether those states are occupied is a separate question.
cards.example: If a small 0.1 eV interval contains 20 states, its average density of states is 200 states per eV.
cards.bridge: Multiply the density of states by the occupation probability to count occupied states. The density depends on whether the gas is one- or three-dimensional.

cards.title: Fermi energy and DOS in one dimension
cards.legend: Let \(s\) label a positive-integer spatial level and \(\mathcal N(E)\) count spin states up to E. Use the many-level continuum approximation.

phases.name: Count
phases.why: each spatial level has two spin states

phases.name: Fermi
phases.why: the count at the Fermi energy equals N

steps.note: Start from the allowed box energies.
Invert the energy relation.

ask.q: How does the level index scale with E?
options: As the square root of E
ask.why: Energy is proportional to the square of the level index.

steps.note: Include both spin states per orbital.

ask.q: Which factor accounts for the two spin states?
ask.why: Each spatial orbital contributes two available spin states.

steps.note: All states up to the Fermi level are filled.
Solve for the one-dimensional Fermi energy.

ask.q: At fixed length, how does E_F scale with N?
options: As the square root of N
ask.why: The number of filled one-dimensional states scales with the Fermi wave number.

steps.note: Return to the cumulative count and differentiate.
This counts both spins and is a whole-box DOS.

ask.q: What is the one-dimensional DOS dependence on E?
ask.why: Differentiating a square-root state count gives an inverse-square-root DOS.

cards.title: Total energy in one dimension
cards.body: For even N, use \(\sum_{s=1}^M s^2=M(M+1)(2M+1)/6\). Keeping the leading \(M^3/3\) term for large N gives \(U/N=E_F/3\).

cards.title: Three-dimensional state counting
cards.body: Periodic boundary conditions assign one spatial state per \((2\pi)^3/V\) of k-space volume. The prefactor 2 counts spins. At zero temperature, fill a sphere of radius \(k_F\).

cards.title: The three-dimensional Fermi energy
cards.body: Here \(n=N/V\) is a volume density. Set \(N=Vk_F^3/(3\pi^2)\), solve for \(k_F\), then use \(E=\hbar^2 k^2/(2m)\). Do not substitute a line density into this formula.

cards.title: Three-dimensional DOS
cards.body: Insert \(k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar\) into \(\mathcal N(k)\), then differentiate with respect to E. This includes both spins. Divide by V for DOS per unit volume.

cards.title: Available states and occupied states
cards.body: At zero temperature f is a step: one below \(E_F\), zero above it. At finite temperature the chemical potential \(\mu(T)\) replaces its zero-temperature limit; \(f(\mu)=1/2\).

cards.title: Total energy in three dimensions
cards.body: Writing \(D(E)=C\sqrt E\), integrate to get \(N=2CE_F^{3/2}/3\) and \(U=2CE_F^{5/2}/5\). Their ratio gives \(U/N=3E_F/5\).

cards.title: Keep the dimensions distinct
cards.body: In 1D the DOS decreases as inverse square root of energy and mean energy is E_F/3. In 3D the DOS grows as square root of energy and mean energy is 3E_F/5. Both include the same spin factor.

cards.title: A clean filling example
cards.body: Exactly: \(U=2(E_1+4E_1+9E_1)\). With only three occupied levels, use the discrete sum, not the large-N approximation \(NE_F/3\).

cards.q: Which dependence is correct for the three-dimensional free-electron DOS?
cards.why: The 3D state count grows as E to the power 3/2, so its derivative grows as the square root.

cards.q: The DOS multiplied by the Fermi function gives the density of ____ states.
cards.why: DOS counts available states; f gives their occupation probability.

cards.q: For a large three-dimensional free-electron gas with \(E_F=5\) eV at zero temperature, what is U/N in eV?
cards.why: The three-dimensional mean energy is \(3E_F/5=3\) eV.

sheets.title: Applications of the electron gas
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §5.3, pp.168–170, with §§5.1–5.2 context; FYUGP Module II, Unit 9.

cards.title: Thermal response · the top layer can change
cards.meaning: The Fermi temperature is the temperature scale corresponding to the Fermi energy.
cards.picture: At temperatures far below this scale, the electron sea is filled almost up to its zero-temperature edge. Heating mainly changes occupations close to that edge, where empty states are available.
cards.example: A metal with a Fermi temperature near 60000 K is still strongly degenerate at 300 K.
cards.bridge: This explains why the electronic heat capacity is much smaller than the classical prediction that treats all electrons as thermally active.

cards.label: Solids · 4 of 9 · 16 min
cards.title: Why most electrons cannot absorb heat
cards.body: For T far below the Fermi temperature, states deep in the filled sea have no nearby empty final states. Only electrons within an energy of order k_B T of the Fermi level are thermally active.

cards.title: Define the Fermi temperature
cards.body: The thermally active fraction is of order \(T/T_F\) for a degenerate gas. This is small in ordinary metals at room temperature; classical equipartition incorrectly treats all electrons as active.

cards.title: Estimate electronic heat capacity
cards.body: Order of magnitude: about \(N(T/T_F)\) electrons can acquire energy of order \(k_BT\). Thus the electronic contribution is small, linear in T, and tends to zero as T tends to zero.

cards.title: Separate electronic and lattice heat
cards.body: The electron-gas model describes the electronic contribution. The crystal lattice contributes separately. Do not identify the measured total heat capacity of a metal with the electron term alone.

cards.title: Room-temperature scale
cards.body: With \(k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}\) eV/K, at 300 K the ratio \(T/T_F\approx0.0052\). Only a small fraction of the sea can change occupation thermally.

cards.title: Transport is also controlled near E_F
cards.body: A field slightly changes occupation near the Fermi surface. Pauli exclusion restricts final states; quantum electrons have a characteristic Fermi speed even when their mean drift is zero.

cards.title: What remains outside the free model
cards.body: Quantum statistics repairs the heat-capacity scale, but a constant interior potential still misses band gaps. Explaining why different solids are metals or insulators requires the lattice's periodic potential.

cards.q: Which electrons chiefly change their occupations when a degenerate electron gas is heated slightly?
cards.why: Nearby empty states are available chiefly near the Fermi surface.

cards.q: At low temperature the electronic heat capacity is approximately ____ in T.
cards.why: The fraction of electrons that can be thermally excited grows in proportion to T.

cards.q: Using the order-of-magnitude active fraction T/T_F, what percentage is active at T = 300 K and T_F = 60000 K?
cards.why: The fraction is 0.005, or 0.5 percent. This is a scale estimate, not an exact count.

sections.title: Properties of Solids · Bloch waves, bands and effective mass

sheets.title: Band theory and Bloch's theorem
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §§6.1–6.2 and §6.3.2, pp.175–180, 186–187; FYUGP Module II, Unit 10.

cards.title: Energy bands · allowed stretches of energy
cards.meaning: An energy band is a continuous interval of allowed electron energies in a crystal; a band gap is an interval between bands with no allowed bulk electron energies.
cards.picture: The repeating atomic arrangement produces a repeating potential. Electron waves in this potential can propagate at some energies but not at others.
cards.example: A semiconductor has a filled valence band separated from an empty conduction band at zero temperature.
cards.bridge: Bloch's theorem describes the form of a wave in the repeating potential; the Kronig–Penney model demonstrates where bands and gaps come from.

cards.label: Solids · 5 of 9 · 18 min
cards.title: What are periodic potentials and bands?
cards.body: A band is an interval of allowed electron energies; a gap is a forbidden interval. Repeating ions produce a periodic potential, a potential-energy function that repeats after a lattice translation.

cards.title: State Bloch's theorem
cards.body: A crystal energy eigenstate can be chosen as a plane wave times a lattice-periodic function. The wave function itself need not be periodic; translation multiplies it by \(e^{ika}\).

cards.title: From translation symmetry to Bloch form
cards.legend: Define \(T_a\psi(x)=\psi(x+a)\). For an ideal periodic crystal, H commutes with the unitary translation T_a, so energy states can be chosen as translation eigenstates.

phases.name: Translation
phases.why: choose simultaneous energy and translation states

phases.name: Phase
phases.why: unitarity makes the eigenvalue a phase

steps.note: Choose a translation eigenstate within the energy eigenspace.

ask.q: Which symmetry allows this choice?
options: Commutation of H with lattice translation
ask.why: Commuting symmetry operators preserve energy eigenspaces.

steps.note: Write the translation in coordinate space.
A unitary translation has unit-modulus eigenvalues.

ask.q: Why is the translation eigenvalue a phase?
ask.why: A unitary operation cannot change the norm of an eigenstate.

steps.note: An allowed bulk Bloch state has real k.
Define a function with the plane-wave phase removed.

ask.q: Which factor removes the phase from psi?
ask.why: The opposite phase cancels the plane-wave factor.

steps.note: Insert the translation law.
The factors containing a cancel.
The remaining factor has lattice periodicity.

ask.q: What repeats after one lattice spacing?
options: Every energy value in free space
ask.why: The Bloch amplitude is periodic even though the full wave function may acquire a phase.

cards.title: Probability density repeats
cards.body: The translation phase has unit modulus, so it cancels from the squared amplitude. A nonconstant lattice-periodic probability density is compatible with a Bloch wave.

cards.title: Free electrons are the limiting case
cards.body: When the periodic potential is removed, the periodic factor can be constant and the state becomes a plane wave. Nonzero lattice modulation couples electron waves and can open gaps.

cards.title: Equivalent wave-vector labels
cards.body: For each band j, k is defined modulo a reciprocal lattice vector. A first-zone interval has width \(2\pi/a\); the reduced-zone description folds all bands into that interval.

cards.title: Count states in a band
cards.body: With periodic boundary conditions and \(N_c\) primitive cells, each band has \(N_c\) distinct spatial k states. Including two spins, it can hold \(2N_c\) electrons. Count a zone endpoint only once.

cards.title: A translation-phase example
cards.body: At this zone-boundary phase the wave function changes sign, while its probability density stays unchanged. It need not vanish.

cards.q: Which factor in a Bloch function has the lattice periodicity?
cards.why: Bloch's theorem writes the state as a plane-wave phase times a lattice-periodic amplitude.

cards.q: A periodic lattice potential leads to allowed energy bands and forbidden energy ____.
cards.why: Periodic scattering prevents propagating bulk solutions in some energy intervals.

cards.q: For a crystal with 100 primitive cells, how many electrons can one spin-degenerate band accommodate?
cards.why: There is one spatial state per cell in a band and two possible spin states per spatial state.

sheets.title: The Kronig–Penney model
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §6.3, pp.180–186; FYUGP Module II, Unit 10.

cards.title: Kronig–Penney · a repeating barrier model
cards.meaning: The Kronig–Penney model is a simplified one-dimensional crystal made from a repeating sequence of potential wells and barriers.
cards.picture: Instead of using the full atomic potential, draw identical flat-bottomed wells separated by identical rectangular barriers. Match the electron wave across each boundary.
cards.example: Some electron energies allow the wave to repeat from cell to cell with a phase change; others fall in gaps.
cards.bridge: Combining boundary matching with Bloch's condition gives the allowed-band equation.

cards.label: Solids · 6 of 9 · 24 min
cards.title: What is the Kronig–Penney model?
cards.body: The Kronig–Penney model describes electrons in a repeating array of square wells and barriers. Each well has width a; each barrier has width b and height V_0. The period is a + b.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Periodic square potential with wells of width a and barriers of width b"><line x1="20" y1="145" x2="244" y2="145" class="gk" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="20,120 50,120 50,55 75,55 75,120 125,120 125,55 150,55 150,120 200,120 200,55 225,55 225,120 244,120" class="lk" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="75" y1="138" x2="125" y2="138" class="hk" stroke-width="3"/><text x="100" y="163" class="t" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">a</text><text x="138" y="43" class="t" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">b</text><text x="28" y="58" class="t" font-size="13">V₀</text><text x="240" y="164" class="t" font-size="13">x</text></svg>

cards.title: Solve the two regions
cards.body: For \(0<E<V_0\), define \(\alpha=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar\) and \(\beta=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar\). The well equation is \(\psi_w''=-\alpha^2\psi_w\); the barrier equation is \(\psi_b''=\beta^2\psi_b\).

cards.title: The four matching conditions
cards.body: Choose a barrier on \(-b<x<0\) and a well on \(0<x<a\). Across the cell, impose \(\psi_w(a)=e^{ikd}\psi_b(-b)\) and \(\psi_w'(a)=e^{ikd}\psi_b'(-b)\). These four homogeneous equations need a nonzero solution.

cards.title: Propagation through one well and barrier
cards.tex: W=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha a&\sin\alpha a/\alpha\\-\alpha\sin\alpha a&\cos\alpha a\end{pmatrix},\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}\cosh\beta b&\sinh\beta b/\beta\\\beta\sinh\beta b&\cosh\beta b\end{pmatrix}
cards.body: These propagate the column \((\psi,\psi')\). Each matrix has determinant one. Their product M propagates by a full cell; Bloch's condition makes its eigenvalues \(e^{ikd}\) and \(e^{-ikd}\).

cards.title: Derive the finite-barrier band condition
cards.legend: Let \(c=\cos\alpha a\), \(s=\sin\alpha a\), \(C=\cosh\beta b\), \(S=\sinh\beta b\). Use the well and barrier propagation matrices above.

phases.name: Trace
phases.why: the diagonal sum fixes the eigenvalue sum

steps.note: Propagate through one well followed by one barrier.

ask.q: Which vector is propagated through the cell?
ask.why: Continuity of psi and psi prime supplies the interface matching data.

steps.note: Use matrix multiplication for the two diagonal entries.

ask.q: What does the matrix trace sum?
ask.why: The trace is the sum of diagonal entries and equals the sum of eigenvalues.

steps.note: Insert the well and barrier matrix elements.
Collect the equal cosine terms.
Use the two Bloch eigenvalues.

ask.q: What is the sum of the two Bloch eigenvalues?
ask.why: The two unit-modulus translation eigenvalues are complex conjugate phases.

steps.note: Divide by two and collect the coefficient.

move.by: C=\cosh\beta b,\ S=\sinh\beta b,\ c=\cos\alpha a,\ s=\sin\alpha a

steps.note: Restore the original trigonometric and hyperbolic factors.

ask.q: For real k, what range must the right side lie in?
ask.why: The cosine of a real wave-vector phase cannot exceed unity in magnitude.

cards.title: Take the narrow-barrier limit
cards.body: Let \(b\to0\), \(V_0\to\infty\), holding \(g=V_0b\) fixed. Then \(\cosh\beta b\to1\), \(\sinh\beta b\sim\beta b\), and \((\beta^2-\alpha^2)b/(2\alpha)\to mg/(\hbar^2\alpha)\). Also d tends to a.

cards.title: Read off bands and gaps
cards.body: Here \(z=\alpha a\), proportional to \(\sqrt E\). If \(|F|>1\), no real k solves the bulk equation: that energy lies in a gap. The limit at z = 0 is \(F(0)=1+P\).

cards.title: Change the barrier strength
cards.body: At P = 0 the free-electron result returns and the gaps close. Stronger barriers generally narrow a given allowed band. In the infinite-barrier limit, isolated-well levels replace broad bands.

cards.title: Three zone descriptions
cards.body: Reduced-zone plots place all bands inside the first zone. Extended-zone plots continue successive bands across zones. Repeated-zone plots repeat the same band structure. These relabel the same states.

cards.title: Test one energy without solving for k
cards.body: Since this exceeds one, the energy is forbidden for propagating bulk states. By contrast z = pi gives F = minus one, a band-edge condition.

cards.q: The Kronig–Penney right side has value 1.2. What does that imply for a real Bloch wave vector?
options: No real k; a band gap
cards.why: A real cosine cannot equal 1.2.

cards.q: The narrow-barrier limit keeps the barrier ____ V_0 b finite.
cards.why: The product of height and width fixes the finite delta-barrier strength.

cards.q: For P = 0 and z = pi/3, what is F(z)?
cards.why: The barrier term vanishes, leaving cosine of pi/3, which is 0.5.

sheets.title: Velocity and effective mass
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §6.4, pp.187–191; FYUGP Module II, Unit 10.

cards.title: Effective mass · response inside a crystal
cards.meaning: Effective mass is the mass-like parameter that describes how a carrier accelerates under an applied force while moving in a crystal band.
cards.picture: The lattice changes how an electron responds to a force. We include that band response in an effective mass so that acceleration can still be written as force divided by mass.
cards.example: If the effective mass is twice the free-electron mass, the same force produces half the acceleration in this model.
cards.bridge: Band slope determines group velocity; band curvature determines effective mass. The electron's intrinsic mass has not changed.

cards.label: Solids · 7 of 9 · 18 min
cards.title: What is group velocity?
cards.body: Group velocity is the velocity at which an electron wave packet travels. It equals the slope of the band energy against wave vector, divided by hbar.

cards.title: Slope and curvature are different
cards.body: At a band extremum the slope and group velocity vanish. Curvature determines effective mass: upward curvature gives positive mass, downward curvature gives negative electron mass.
