cards.title: Force changes crystal momentum
cards.body: This is the semiclassical equation for a wave packet within one band, neglecting interband transitions. For an electron in an electric field, \(F_{\mathrm{ext}}=-eE\).

cards.title: Derive the effective-mass formula
cards.legend: One spatial dimension, a differentiable band E(k), and external force F. Denote acceleration by a_acc to distinguish it from a lattice spacing.

phases.name: Force
phases.why: use the rate of change of k

steps.note: Start from the group velocity.
Differentiate along the wave-packet motion.

ask.q: Which time-dependent variable changes the band slope?
ask.why: The applied force moves the wave packet through k space.

steps.note: Apply the chain rule.

ask.q: Which energy derivative appears in the acceleration?
ask.why: Differentiating the slope once more with respect to k gives the curvature.

steps.note: Insert the crystal-momentum equation.

ask.q: Which dynamical law is used here?
ask.why: Force is the time derivative of crystal momentum hbar k.

steps.note: Name the acceleration.
Identify the inverse effective mass.

ask.q: What sign does m* have for negative curvature?
ask.why: The sign of the inverse mass is the sign of the band curvature.

steps.note: Invert when the curvature is nonzero.

cards.title: Check the free-electron limit
cards.body: The first derivative gives the velocity and the constant second derivative \(\hbar^2/m\) returns the ordinary electron mass.

cards.title: At an inflection point
cards.body: The inverse mass vanishes; the scalar mass diverges in this ideal one-band description. The velocity can be nonzero there because the first derivative need not vanish.

cards.title: Negative electron mass and holes
cards.body: Near a band maximum the electron has negative curvature mass. A missing electron in a nearly filled band is described as a hole with positive charge and positive effective mass.

cards.title: A band-curvature example
cards.body: The curvature is \(\hbar^2/(2m)\), half the free-electron curvature. Under the same external force the acceleration is half as large.

cards.q: Which feature of E(k) determines group velocity?
options: The value of E without a derivative
cards.why: Group velocity is one over hbar times the first derivative.

cards.q: Effective mass is inversely proportional to band ____.
cards.why: The scalar mass is hbar squared divided by the second derivative of E with respect to k.

cards.q: If the curvature is \(2\hbar^2/m\), what is the ratio \(m^*/m\)?
cards.why: Substituting the curvature gives m star equal to m/2.

sections.title: Properties of Solids · Metals, insulators and semiconductors

sheets.title: Metal, insulator or semiconductor?
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §6.5, pp.191–193; FYUGP Module II, Unit 11.

cards.title: Three material types · which states can carry current?
cards.meaning: Metals conduct readily, insulators conduct very poorly under ordinary conditions, and semiconductors have conduction that can be strongly controlled by temperature and doping.
cards.picture: To respond to a weak field, electrons need nearby unoccupied states. Metals have these available; in a semiconductor or insulator, a gap separates full and empty bands at zero temperature.
cards.example: Copper is a metal; pure silicon is a semiconductor. Their different band fillings and gaps explain their different electrical responses.
cards.bridge: The band picture gives the microscopic explanation behind the everyday labels.

cards.label: Solids · 8 of 9 · 14 min
cards.title: Conduction needs available nearby states
cards.body: Band filling and accessible empty states determine conduction. A partly filled band can change its occupation under a weak field. A full isolated band cannot carry a net current in this ordinary band picture.

cards.title: Why a full band gives zero net current
cards.body: For a filled band, velocities from opposite k states cancel. With all states occupied, a weak field cannot simply shift electrons into neighboring occupied states. A hole or an accessible higher band changes this.

cards.title: Metals
cards.body: A metal has a partially filled band, or overlapping bands that leave accessible states at the Fermi energy. Electrons can redistribute among nearby states with very small energy changes.

cards.title: Insulators and semiconductors
cards.body: At zero temperature both have filled valence bands and empty conduction bands. An ordinary semiconductor has a gap small enough for practical thermal excitation or doping; an insulator has a much less accessible gap.

cards.title: Compare the band diagrams
cards.body: Filled regions are shown below empty regions. The semiconductor has a narrower forbidden interval than the insulator. The drawings are schematic and their widths do not represent DOS.

cards.title: The forbidden energy interval
cards.body: Here \(E_c\) is the conduction-band minimum and \(E_v\) the valence-band maximum. The gap is an energy difference, not the width of a real-space separation.

cards.title: Temperature trends
cards.body: In ordinary metals, stronger scattering typically raises resistivity as temperature rises. In an intrinsic semiconductor, thermal generation increases carrier numbers and usually lowers resistivity.

cards.title: Compare with the thermal scale
cards.body: A gap of 1 eV is much larger than this scale, yet a small thermally excited carrier population can still exist. There is no universal sharp gap value that separates every semiconductor from every insulator.

cards.q: Which situation produces an ordinary band metal?
options: A full isolated band and a large gap
An empty valence band with no electrons
cards.why: A partly filled band offers nearby empty states that allow redistribution and current.

cards.q: The highest occupied band at zero temperature in an ordinary semiconductor is the ____ band.
cards.why: The valence band is full while the conduction band is empty in the ideal undoped zero-temperature picture.

cards.q: If E_c = 1.4 eV and E_v = 0.2 eV on the same energy reference, what is E_g?
cards.why: Subtract the valence-band maximum from the conduction-band minimum.

sheets.title: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
sheets.source: Puri & Babbar §§7.1–7.3.2, pp.199–204; FYUGP Module III, Unit 12 only.

cards.title: Intrinsic and extrinsic · pure or doped
cards.meaning: An intrinsic semiconductor is undoped material whose carriers are generated as electron–hole pairs. An extrinsic semiconductor contains deliberate impurities that supply extra electrons or holes.
cards.picture: Pure silicon relies on excitation to create mobile carriers. Adding a small amount of phosphorus supplies extra electrons; adding boron produces extra holes.
cards.example: Phosphorus-doped silicon is n-type; boron-doped silicon is p-type.
cards.bridge: Donor and acceptor atoms introduce energy levels in the band gap while keeping the sample electrically neutral overall.

cards.label: Solids · 9 of 9 · 18 min
cards.title: What is an intrinsic semiconductor?
cards.body: An intrinsic semiconductor is an undoped semiconductor whose mobile carriers arise from electron–hole pair excitation. Each excitation creates a conduction electron and a valence-band hole, so n and p are equal.

cards.title: What is a hole?
cards.body: A hole is an unoccupied electron state in a nearly full valence band. As neighboring electrons fill the vacancy, it moves the opposite way and behaves as a positively charged mobile carrier.

cards.title: Generation and recombination
cards.body: Thermal excitation creates electron–hole pairs; recombination removes pairs. At equilibrium the generation and recombination rates match. Electrons and holes can both contribute to current.

cards.title: What is an extrinsic semiconductor?
cards.body: An extrinsic semiconductor is a semiconductor whose carrier population is altered by intentional impurity atoms (dopants). Donors supply electrons; acceptors create holes. The material remains neutral overall.

cards.title: Donors make n-type material
cards.body: In silicon, a group-V donor such as phosphorus has a fifth valence electron left after four bonds form. A small thermal energy ionizes it into the conduction band, leaving a fixed positive donor ion.

cards.title: Acceptors make p-type material
cards.body: A group-III dopant such as boron can accept a valence electron to complete bonding. This leaves a mobile valence-band hole and a fixed negative acceptor ion.

cards.title: Donor and acceptor energy levels
cards.body: A shallow donor level lies just below the conduction edge; a shallow acceptor level lies just above the valence edge. These small ionization energies differ from the host's full band gap.

cards.title: Compare ionization energies
cards.body: For example, \(E_c-E_D=0.04\) eV is much less than a host gap of 1.1 eV. A donor can release a carrier without exciting an electron across the entire host gap.

cards.title: Keep carrier and ion charges distinct
cards.body: n-type does not mean a negatively charged specimen. A donated electron is balanced by a positive fixed donor ion. In p-type material, the positive hole is balanced by a negative fixed acceptor ion.

cards.title: A carrier-counting example
cards.body: In an intrinsic sample, generation adds equal numbers of each carrier. In an n-type sample with ionized donors dominating, most mobile carriers are electrons; holes remain the minority.

cards.q: Which dopant produces n-type silicon in the usual substitutional picture?
cards.why: Phosphorus is pentavalent and donates an extra electron after forming four silicon bonds.

cards.q: The majority mobile carriers in p-type silicon are ____.
cards.why: Acceptor dopants remove electrons from valence bonding states, leaving mobile holes.

cards.q: Where is a shallow donor level?
options: At every energy in the gap
cards.why: A donor electron requires only a small energy to enter the conduction band.

cards.q: An intrinsic sample has 250 conduction electrons created by pair excitation. How many corresponding holes were created?
cards.why: Each excitation across the gap creates one conduction electron and one valence-band hole.
